protocol.purpose: Ten additional, distinct, three-provider rewrite trials on the frozen public garden example. Local research, not ten production runs.
protocol.selection_rule: Consider only candidates that clear source-fidelity audit and protected-value checks. Prefer candidates strictly lower than the previous-best baseline on BOTH fixed detectors. Among those minimize max(Desklib/baselineDesklib,Vanguard/baselineVanguard). Otherwise retain baseline and report single-detector changes separately. Scores do not establish authorship or guarantee other detector outcomes.
protocol.scoring: Exact final reviewed and cleaned text joined with two newlines, unchanged title included once. Fixed Desklib and Vanguard revisions, no truncation. Record SHA256. No score feedback given to writer.

trials.name: Watering first
trials.instruction: Begin with the unresolved question of being away for 4 days. Develop the garden idea through that practical concern, bringing in the possible self-watering container, its unanswered suitability and cost questions, and other preparations where relevant. The absence is hypothetical, not a booked trip.

trials.name: Budget first
trials.instruction: Explain this as a small experiment with a $60 first-stage ceiling. Connect what that must buy, what is already owned, and what would be reduced if prices are higher. Let planting and maintenance decisions develop from that limited commitment. Do not change the intended 3 containers.

trials.name: Balcony first
trials.instruction: Start with the actual balcony: morning sunlight, afternoon shade and limited room around the door. Explain how I intend to fit the proposed garden into that space, integrating drainage, plant choices and maintenance without separate essay-style topic sections. Do not invent dimensions, sunlight hours or complaints.

trials.name: Tentative plant choices
trials.instruction: Build the note around basil, mint and parsley as provisional choices. Show what remains to be learned before choosing everything, then connect containers, watering during travel and the spending limit. Keep uncertainty alive instead of resolving it. No new horticultural advice.

trials.name: Conditional start date
trials.instruction: Open with the hoped-for 18 April start, immediately preserving its conditions. Work backward through the checks that remain, distinguishing what I know from what I still need to decide. Finish with the planned first-month review without a summary slogan. This is a hope, not a deadline.

trials.name: Maintenance before expansion
trials.instruction: Organize the note around how little I want to commit initially and what I need to learn before expanding. Connect 3 containers, travel and watering, the fixed initial budget, and the first-month review. Introduce the physical balcony and herbs as the concrete setting. Expansion is only a possibility after success; preserve enjoyment as a review criterion.

trials.name: Pair decisions with limits
trials.instruction: Interleave each proposed action with its source-stated condition or limitation: preferred herbs with unmeasured sunlight, containers with space and drainage, spending with the already-owned can, watering with possible absence, and starting with weather and checks. Reorganize these pairs into a coherent note. Do not invent causal dependencies between unrelated checks.

trials.name: Continuous personal note
trials.instruction: Write this as a continuous personal note in two or three paragraphs. Let related details meet within paragraphs instead of assigning one paragraph to each original topic. Use ordinary phrasing and retain every substantive detail; this is recomposition, not summarization. Preserve spring timing, cooking motivation and the enjoyment review.

trials.name: Conversational explanation
trials.instruction: Explain the proposed garden in the language I could comfortably use in ordinary conversation. Keep first person and precise details. Prefer everyday verbs to planning terminology, but add no greeting, named listener, anecdotes, excitement or invented personality. Retain intentions and uncertainty.

trials.name: Unfinished working thought
trials.instruction: Let the note develop through the source's genuine unresolved decisions. State an intention, then qualify it where the source does, and continue to the next related concern. Keep it readable and complete without making every paragraph neatly introduce, explain and conclude a topic. No artificial hesitation, rhetorical questions or invented doubts.

audit.review_method: Direct whole-document source-versus-final-output review against 32 claims, plus unsupported additions, modality, and obvious prose quality. Candidate detector scores were not consulted.
audit.eligibility_rule: All source claims pass without unresolved ambiguity; no unsupported addition, obvious publication-blocking prose defect, title or hash mismatch, machine rejection, or protected-value failure. A changed candidate must be reviewed and scored afresh.

source.text: My balcony garden plan

I am planning to grow herbs on my balcony this spring because I would like to have fresh ingredients available when I cook. The balcony receives direct sunlight in the morning, but the neighboring building shades it during the afternoon. I have not measured the exact amount of sunlight yet, so I need to do that before choosing all the plants. My initial preference is for basil, mint, and parsley, although I may change this list after learning more about their needs.

The space is limited, and I do not want the pots to make it difficult to open the balcony door. I intend to start with 3 containers rather than filling the entire area immediately. This should allow me to learn how much maintenance is required before making a larger commitment. I also need to check that the containers have drainage holes and that any water underneath them will not cause problems for my downstairs neighbor.

My budget for the first stage is $60. That amount needs to cover the containers, potting mix, and the plants themselves. I already own a small watering can, so I do not expect to purchase another one. If the total cost is higher than expected, I will reduce the number of plants rather than increase the budget. I want this to remain a manageable experiment instead of becoming an expensive project.

Watering is the part I am most uncertain about. I sometimes travel for work, and I cannot assume that a neighbor will always be available to help. Before buying anything, I will consider what would happen if I were away for 4 days. A simple self-watering container might help, but I have not compared prices or checked whether it would be suitable for the plants I want.

I hope to begin on 18 April, provided that the weather is suitable and I have finished the necessary checks. After the first month, I will review which plants are doing well and whether I am enjoying the routine. If the experiment is successful, I may add another herb later. For now, my goal is simply to learn and grow a small amount of food without taking on more than I can comfortably maintain.

output.text: My balcony garden plan

Before buying anything, I will consider what would happen if I were away for 4 days. Watering is the part I’m least sure about: I sometimes travel for work, and I can’t count on a neighbor always being available to help. A simple self-watering container might be useful, but I haven’t compared prices or checked whether it would suit the plants I want to grow.

I’m planning a small balcony herb garden this spring so I can have fresh ingredients available when I cook. Basil, mint, and parsley are my first choices, though that list may change as I learn more about what they need. The balcony gets direct morning sun, then shade from the neighboring building in the afternoon. I still need to measure how much sunlight it gets before choosing all the plants.

With limited space, I want to keep the pots out of the way of the balcony door so it remains easy to open. I intend to start with 3 containers rather than fill the whole area, giving myself a chance to find out how much maintenance is involved before committing to more. I also need to check that the containers have drainage holes and that water collecting underneath them won’t cause problems for the downstairs neighbor.

My budget for this first stage is $60, covering the containers, potting mix, and plants. I already have a small watering can and don’t expect to purchase another. If the total comes to more than I expect, I’ll buy fewer plants rather than increase the budget. I want this to remain a manageable experiment, not turn into an expensive project.

I hope to begin on 18 April, as long as the weather is suitable and I’ve finished the necessary checks. After the first month, I’ll look at which plants are doing well and whether I enjoy the routine. If it works out, I may add another herb later. For now, I just want to learn and grow a little food without taking on more than I can comfortably maintain.

source.text: My balcony garden plan

I am planning to grow herbs on my balcony this spring because I would like to have fresh ingredients available when I cook. The balcony receives direct sunlight in the morning, but the neighboring building shades it during the afternoon. I have not measured the exact amount of sunlight yet, so I need to do that before choosing all the plants. My initial preference is for basil, mint, and parsley, although I may change this list after learning more about their needs.

The space is limited, and I do not want the pots to make it difficult to open the balcony door. I intend to start with 3 containers rather than filling the entire area immediately. This should allow me to learn how much maintenance is required before making a larger commitment. I also need to check that the containers have drainage holes and that any water underneath them will not cause problems for my downstairs neighbor.

My budget for the first stage is $60. That amount needs to cover the containers, potting mix, and the plants themselves. I already own a small watering can, so I do not expect to purchase another one. If the total cost is higher than expected, I will reduce the number of plants rather than increase the budget. I want this to remain a manageable experiment instead of becoming an expensive project.

Watering is the part I am most uncertain about. I sometimes travel for work, and I cannot assume that a neighbor will always be available to help. Before buying anything, I will consider what would happen if I were away for 4 days. A simple self-watering container might help, but I have not compared prices or checked whether it would be suitable for the plants I want.

I hope to begin on 18 April, provided that the weather is suitable and I have finished the necessary checks. After the first month, I will review which plants are doing well and whether I am enjoying the routine. If the experiment is successful, I may add another herb later. For now, my goal is simply to learn and grow a small amount of food without taking on more than I can comfortably maintain.

I plan to grow herbs on my balcony this spring so that I have fresh ingredients on hand when I cook. I want it to stay a manageable experiment rather than an expensive project, . The first-stage budget is $60. That has to cover the containers, the potting mix, and the plants. I already own a small watering can and don't expect to buy another. If the total comes out higher than I expect, I will cut back on the number of plants rather than raise the budget.

I intend to start with 3 containers rather than filling the whole area at once. Space is tight, and I don't want pots getting in the way of opening the balcony door. Starting small should show me how much maintenance this really takes before I commit to anything larger. I also need to check that the containers have drainage holes and that water collecting underneath won't cause problems for my downstairs neighbor.

I haven't measured the exact amount of sunlight yet. The balcony gets direct sun in the morning but is shaded by the neighboring building in the afternoon, and I need to measure it before choosing all the plants. For now I lean toward basil, mint, and parsley, though I may change that list once I know more about what they need.

Watering is what I'm least sure about. I sometimes travel for work and can't count on a neighbor always being available to help. Before buying anything, I will think through what would happen if I were away for 4 days. A simple self-watering container might help, but I haven't compared prices or checked whether it suits the plants I want.

I hope to begin on 18 April, as long as the weather is suitable and I've finished those checks. After the first month I'll look at which plants are doing well and whether I actually enjoy the routine. If it goes well, I may add another herb later. source.text: My balcony garden plan

I am planning to grow herbs on my balcony this spring because I would like to have fresh ingredients available when I cook. The balcony receives direct sunlight in the morning, but the neighboring building shades it during the afternoon. I have not measured the exact amount of sunlight yet, so I need to do that before choosing all the plants. My initial preference is for basil, mint, and parsley, although I may change this list after learning more about their needs.

The space is limited, and I do not want the pots to make it difficult to open the balcony door. I intend to start with 3 containers rather than filling the entire area immediately. This should allow me to learn how much maintenance is required before making a larger commitment. I also need to check that the containers have drainage holes and that any water underneath them will not cause problems for my downstairs neighbor.

My budget for the first stage is $60. That amount needs to cover the containers, potting mix, and the plants themselves. I already own a small watering can, so I do not expect to purchase another one. If the total cost is higher than expected, I will reduce the number of plants rather than increase the budget. I want this to remain a manageable experiment instead of becoming an expensive project.

Watering is the part I am most uncertain about. I sometimes travel for work, and I cannot assume that a neighbor will always be available to help. Before buying anything, I will consider what would happen if I were away for 4 days. A simple self-watering container might help, but I have not compared prices or checked whether it would be suitable for the plants I want.

I hope to begin on 18 April, provided that the weather is suitable and I have finished the necessary checks. After the first month, I will review which plants are doing well and whether I am enjoying the routine. If the experiment is successful, I may add another herb later. For now, my goal is simply to learn and grow a small amount of food without taking on more than I can comfortably maintain.

source.text: My balcony garden plan

I am planning to grow herbs on my balcony this spring because I would like to have fresh ingredients available when I cook. The balcony receives direct sunlight in the morning, but the neighboring building shades it during the afternoon. I have not measured the exact amount of sunlight yet, so I need to do that before choosing all the plants. My initial preference is for basil, mint, and parsley, although I may change this list after learning more about their needs.

The space is limited, and I do not want the pots to make it difficult to open the balcony door. I intend to start with 3 containers rather than filling the entire area immediately. This should allow me to learn how much maintenance is required before making a larger commitment. I also need to check that the containers have drainage holes and that any water underneath them will not cause problems for my downstairs neighbor.

My budget for the first stage is $60. That amount needs to cover the containers, potting mix, and the plants themselves. I already own a small watering can, so I do not expect to purchase another one. If the total cost is higher than expected, I will reduce the number of plants rather than increase the budget. I want this to remain a manageable experiment instead of becoming an expensive project.

Watering is the part I am most uncertain about. I sometimes travel for work, and I cannot assume that a neighbor will always be available to help. Before buying anything, I will consider what would happen if I were away for 4 days. A simple self-watering container might help, but I have not compared prices or checked whether it would be suitable for the plants I want.

I hope to begin on 18 April, provided that the weather is suitable and I have finished the necessary checks. After the first month, I will review which plants are doing well and whether I am enjoying the routine. If the experiment is successful, I may add another herb later. For now, my goal is simply to learn and grow a small amount of food without taking on more than I can comfortably maintain.

output.text: My balcony garden plan

I'm planning to grow herbs on my balcony this spring because I would like to have fresh ingredients available when I cook. The balcony gets direct sunlight in the morning, but the neighboring building shades it in the afternoon. I haven't measured the exact amount of sunlight yet, and I need to do that before choosing all the plants. Basil, mint, and parsley are my first choices, though that list may change once I learn more about what they need.

Space is limited, and I don't want pots getting in the way of opening the balcony door. So I intend to start with 3 containers rather than fill the whole area right away, which should show me how much maintenance is involved before I commit to anything larger. I also need to check that the containers have drainage holes and that water underneath them won't cause problems for my downstairs neighbor.

Watering is the part I'm most unsure about. I sometimes travel for work, and I can't assume a neighbor will always be available to help. Before buying anything, I'll think through what would happen if I were away for 4 days. A simple self-watering container might help, but I haven't compared prices or checked whether one would suit the plants I want.

The budget for this first stage is $60, and it has to cover the containers, potting mix, and plants. I already have a small watering can and don't expect to buy another. If the total comes out higher than I expect, I'll buy fewer plants rather than raise the budget. I want this to stay a manageable experiment, not an expensive project. For now, my goal is to learn and grow a small amount of food without taking on more than I can comfortably maintain.

I hope to begin on 18 April, as long as the weather is suitable and I've finished the necessary checks. After the first month, I'll review which plants are doing well and whether I enjoy the routine. If the experiment is successful, I may add another herb later.

I hope to begin on 18 April, provided that the weather is suitable and I have finished the necessary checks. After the first month, I will review which plants are doing well and whether I am enjoying the routine. If the experiment is successful, I may add another herb later. For now, my goal is simply to learn and grow a small amount of food without taking on more than I can comfortably maintain.

output.text: My balcony garden plan

This spring, I plan to grow herbs on my balcony so I have fresh ingredients to use when cooking. I’d like to start with basil, mint, and parsley, but I haven’t yet measured how much sunlight the balcony gets. There’s direct sun in the morning, while the neighboring building shades it in the afternoon. I need to measure the sunlight before settling on all the plants, and my choices may change as I learn more about their needs.

I intend to begin with 3 containers, rather than filling the entire area immediately. This should allow me to learn how much maintenance is required before making a larger commitment. Space is limited, and I do not want the pots to make it difficult to open the balcony door. I still need to check that the containers have drainage holes and that water underneath them won’t create problems for the downstairs neighbor.

I have a budget of $60 for this first stage, covering the containers, potting mix, and plants. I already own a small watering can, so I don’t expect to need another. If the total costs more than I expect, I’ll cut back on the number of plants rather than raise the budget. I want to keep this a manageable experiment rather than an expensive project.

Watering is the part I am most uncertain about. I sometimes travel for work, and I cannot assume that a neighbor will always be available to help. Before I buy anything, I’ll consider what would happen if I were away for 4 days. A simple self-watering container might be useful, though I haven’t compared prices or checked whether it would suit the plants I want.

I hope to start on 18 April, provided the weather is suitable and I have finished the necessary checks. For now, my goal is simply to learn and grow a small amount of food without taking on more than I can comfortably maintain. After the first month, I’ll look at which plants are doing well and whether I enjoy the routine. If the experiment succeeds, I may add another herb later.

I am planning to grow herbs on my balcony this spring because I would like to have fresh ingredients available when I cook. The balcony receives direct sunlight in the morning, but the neighboring building shades it during the afternoon. I have not measured the exact amount of sunlight yet, so I need to do that before choosing all the plants. My initial preference is for basil, mint, and parsley, although I may change this list after learning more about their needs.

The space is limited, and I do not want the pots to make it difficult to open the balcony door. I intend to start with 3 containers rather than filling the entire area immediately. This should allow me to learn how much maintenance is required before making a larger commitment. I also need to check that the containers have drainage holes and that any water underneath them will not cause problems for my downstairs neighbor.

My budget for the first stage is $60. That amount needs to cover the containers, potting mix, and the plants themselves. I already own a small watering can, so I do not expect to purchase another one. If the total cost is higher than expected, I will reduce the number of plants rather than increase the budget. I want this to remain a manageable experiment instead of becoming an expensive project.

Watering is the part I am most uncertain about. I sometimes travel for work, and I cannot assume that a neighbor will always be available to help. Before buying anything, I will consider what would happen if I were away for 4 days. A simple self-watering container might help, but I have not compared prices or checked whether it would be suitable for the plants I want.

I hope to begin on 18 April, provided that the weather is suitable and I have finished the necessary checks. After the first month, I will review which plants are doing well and whether I am enjoying the routine. If the experiment is successful, I may add another herb later. For now, my goal is simply to learn and grow a small amount of food without taking on more than I can comfortably maintain.

output.text: My balcony garden plan

I'm planning to grow herbs on my balcony this spring so I can have fresh ingredients on hand when I'm cooking. The balcony gets direct sunlight in the morning, but the neighboring building shades it in the afternoon, and I haven't measured exactly how much light it gets. I need to do that before choosing all the plants. Basil, mint, and parsley are my first choices, though the list may change once I learn more about what they need. Space is limited too, and I don't want pots getting in the way of opening the balcony door, so I intend to start with 3 containers rather than fill the whole area right away. That should let me see how much maintenance is involved before I commit to anything larger. I also need to check that the containers have drainage holes and that water underneath them won't cause problems for my downstairs neighbor.

The budget for this first stage is $60, and it has to cover the containers, the potting mix, and the plants. I already have a small watering can and don't expect to buy another. If the total comes out higher than I expect, I'll buy fewer plants rather than raise the budget, because I want this to stay a manageable experiment and not turn into an expensive project. Watering is the part I'm least sure about. I sometimes travel for work, and I can't assume a neighbor will always be available to help. Before buying anything, I'll think through what would happen if I were away for 4 days. A simple self-watering container might help, but I haven't compared prices or checked whether one would suit the plants I want.

I hope to begin on 18 April, as long as the weather is suitable and I've finished the necessary checks. After the first month, I'll review which plants are doing well and whether I enjoy the routine. If it works out, I may add another herb later. For now, my goal is to learn and to grow a small amount of food without taking on more than I can comfortably maintain.

source.text: My balcony garden plan

I am planning to grow herbs on my balcony this spring because I would like to have fresh ingredients available when I cook. The balcony receives direct sunlight in the morning, but the neighboring building shades it during the afternoon. I have not measured the exact amount of sunlight yet, so I need to do that before choosing all the plants. My initial preference is for basil, mint, and parsley, although I may change this list after learning more about their needs.

The space is limited, and I do not want the pots to make it difficult to open the balcony door. I intend to start with 3 containers rather than filling the entire area immediately. This should allow me to learn how much maintenance is required before making a larger commitment. I also need to check that the containers have drainage holes and that any water underneath them will not cause problems for my downstairs neighbor.

My budget for the first stage is $60. That amount needs to cover the containers, potting mix, and the plants themselves. I already own a small watering can, so I do not expect to purchase another one. If the total cost is higher than expected, I will reduce the number of plants rather than increase the budget. I want this to remain a manageable experiment instead of becoming an expensive project.

Watering is the part I am most uncertain about. I sometimes travel for work, and I cannot assume that a neighbor will always be available to help. Before buying anything, I will consider what would happen if I were away for 4 days. A simple self-watering container might help, but I have not compared prices or checked whether it would be suitable for the plants I want.

I hope to begin on 18 April, provided that the weather is suitable and I have finished the necessary checks. After the first month, I will review which plants are doing well and whether I am enjoying the routine. If the experiment is successful, I may add another herb later. For now, my goal is simply to learn and grow a small amount of food without taking on more than I can comfortably maintain.

output.text: My balcony garden plan

I’m planning to grow herbs on my balcony this spring so I have fresh ingredients available when I cook. It gets direct sunlight in the morning, but the neighboring building shades it in the afternoon. I haven’t measured exactly how much sunlight it gets yet, and I need to do that before choosing all the plants. I’m leaning toward basil, mint, and parsley, though I may change that list after learning more about what they need.

I plan to start with 3 containers instead of filling the balcony right away, so I can find out how much care they need before adding more. There isn’t much space, and I don’t want the pots to get in the way of opening the balcony door. I still need to check that the containers have drainage holes and that water underneath them won’t cause problems for the downstairs neighbor.

Watering is the part I’m least sure about. I sometimes travel for work, so I can’t assume a neighbor will always be available to help. Before I buy anything, I’ll think through what would happen if I were away for 4 days. A simple self-watering container might help, but I haven’t compared prices or checked whether it would suit the plants I want.

I have a budget of $60 for this first stage, including containers, potting mix, and plants. I already own a small watering can and don’t expect to need another. If the total costs more than I expect, I’ll buy fewer plants rather than raise the budget. I want a manageable experiment, not an expensive project.

I hope to start on 18 April, if the weather is suitable and I’ve finished the checks I need to make. After the first month, I’ll look at which plants are doing well and whether I’m enjoying the routine. If it works out, I may add another herb later. For now, my goal is to learn and grow a small amount of food without taking on more than I can comfortably care for.

source.text: My balcony garden plan

I am planning to grow herbs on my balcony this spring because I would like to have fresh ingredients available when I cook. The balcony receives direct sunlight in the morning, but the neighboring building shades it during the afternoon. I have not measured the exact amount of sunlight yet, so I need to do that before choosing all the plants. My initial preference is for basil, mint, and parsley, although I may change this list after learning more about their needs.

The space is limited, and I do not want the pots to make it difficult to open the balcony door. I intend to start with 3 containers rather than filling the entire area immediately. This should allow me to learn how much maintenance is required before making a larger commitment. I also need to check that the containers have drainage holes and that any water underneath them will not cause problems for my downstairs neighbor.

My budget for the first stage is $60. That amount needs to cover the containers, potting mix, and the plants themselves. I already own a small watering can, so I do not expect to purchase another one. If the total cost is higher than expected, I will reduce the number of plants rather than increase the budget. I want this to remain a manageable experiment instead of becoming an expensive project.

Watering is the part I am most uncertain about. I sometimes travel for work, and I cannot assume that a neighbor will always be available to help. Before buying anything, I will consider what would happen if I were away for 4 days. A simple self-watering container might help, but I have not compared prices or checked whether it would be suitable for the plants I want.

I hope to begin on 18 April, provided that the weather is suitable and I have finished the necessary checks. After the first month, I will review which plants are doing well and whether I am enjoying the routine. If the experiment is successful, I may add another herb later. For now, my goal is simply to learn and grow a small amount of food without taking on more than I can comfortably maintain.
